summary: Kam Lasater's talk builds an agent incrementally, starting from a basic OpenAI chat completion and progressively adding components. The stated goal is for attendees to understand the simplest possible agent and gain intuition for how frameworks work under the hood. Lasater defines an agent as LLM, memory, planning, tools, and a while loop, noting memory involves read and write operations and the while loop is really a conditional plus looping. Step Zero is a standard chat completion. Step One introduces a condition via an LLM-as-judge that evaluates whether a response fully answers the question, returning a forced JSON Boolean. Step Two adds a Google search tool using SerpAI, showing how the OpenAI SDK returns tool call instructions that local code must execute and feed back. This step demonstrates a failure where the location parameter rejects arbitrary strings. Step Three refactors tool handling into a separate utils file and adds parallel tool call support using Promise.all, passing function arguments for each call and tracking tool call IDs. Lasater frames tools as text transformations, typically string-to-string. Step Four introduces planning via a to-do list with add, mark-done, check-done, and check-todos tools, plus a browse-web tool using Cheerio and Turndown. A system prompt instructs the assistant to always make a plan first, use tools, mark items complete, create a report, and check goal completion (LLM-as-judge as a tool). The LLM handles looping through tool calls internally, making the main function a single complete-with-tools call. Lasater notes guardrails like limiting iteration count may be needed to prevent infinite loops. The first demo shows the agent creating a to-do plan for learning about building agents without a framework, then executing it: searching Google, browsing blog posts and Pond Data, converting pages to markdown, marking tasks done, checking todos, and getting an LLM-as-judge thumbs up. The agent produces a summary covering core components, tools, memory, loop, and prompt engineering. A second demo shows the agent planning a Saturday date night, searching for activities and dinner options between 6 and 11 p.m., browsing restaurants, marking items done, checking the goal, and outputting activities and dinner suggestions. Lasater acknowledges the agent is not perfect but emphasizes how the components coming together produce interesting behavior. He suggests next steps such as adding a vector database or injecting browsed web pages into a ChromaDB or RAG-like system. He closes by sharing his LinkedIn, slides on his personal site, and code on GitHub, inviting feedback and collaboration.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: An agent minimally consists of LLM, memory, planning, tools, and a while loop, where memory is read/write and the loop is conditional plus iteration
LLM-as-judge serves as the condition: a second LLM call evaluates whether the answer fully satisfies the original question
Tool calls require local code execution: the OpenAI SDK returns tool call instructions but does not execute them; results must be pushed back into the conversation
Tools are best understood as text transformations, typically string-to-string operations
Parallel tool calls can be handled with Promise.all, passing arguments for each call and tracking tool call IDs for LLM traceability
Planning is implemented via a to-do list tool with add, mark-done, check-done, and check-todos operations, driven by a system prompt instructing the LLM to always plan first
Pushing the LLM-as-judge condition as a tool itself lets the LLM handle the while loop internally, reducing the main function to a single complete-with-tools call
Guardrails such as limiting iteration count may be necessary to prevent the LLM from looping indefinitely without converging
The agent produces useful output by autonomously searching, browsing, summarizing, and self-evaluating, though it is not perfect
Suggested next steps include adding a vector database or RAG-like system to store browsed web pages for richer retrieval

sections.title: Introduction and Goals
sections.summary: Kam Lasater introduces the talk with three goals: experience the simplest agent, feel comfortable running and breaking the code, and gain intuition for how agents and frameworks work. Slides and code are available on his website.

sections.title: What is an Agent
sections.summary: Defines an agent as LLM, memory, planning, tools, and a while loop. Mathematically breaks memory into read and write operations and the while loop into conditional and looping, then reorders them into a build plan.

sections.title: Step Zero: Calling an LLM
sections.summary: Demonstrates a standard OpenAI chat completion from the hello world docs, establishing the deterministic baseline.

sections.title: Step One: The Condition (LLM-as-Judge)
sections.summary: Adds a condition by making a second LLM call as a strict critic that determines if the answer fully answers the question, returning a forced JSON Boolean. Demonstrated with the question about average wing speed of a swallow.

sections.title: Step Two: Tools (SerpAI Search)
sections.summary: Introduces a Google search tool via SerpAI for a hoodie shopping query. Shows hand-written JSON tool config with name, descriptions, strict schema, and parameters. Explains that the OpenAI SDK returns tool call instructions but local code must execute them. Demo fails on location parameter validation. Still feels deterministic.

sections.title: Step Three: Refactoring and Parallel Tool Calls
sections.summary: Refactors tool handling into a utils file and adds parallel tool call support using Promise.all. Each tool call response includes a tool call ID for LLM traceability. Frames tools as text transformations, typically string-to-string. Still deterministic after reshuffling.

sections.title: Step Four: Planning via To-Do List
sections.summary: Introduces planning through a to-do list with add, mark-done, check-done, and check-todos tools, plus a browse-web tool using Cheerio and Turndown. A system prompt drives the LLM to always plan first, use tools, mark items complete, create a report, and check goal completion. The LLM-as-judge becomes a tool, the LLM handles looping internally, and the main function reduces to a single complete-with-tools call. Demo shows the agent creating a plan for learning about building agents without a framework.

sections.title: Step Four Demo Execution and Summary Output
sections.summary: The agent executes its to-do plan: searching Google, browsing blog posts and Pond Data, converting pages to markdown, marking tasks done, checking todos, and receiving an LLM-as-judge thumbs up. It produces a summary of building agents without a framework covering core components, tools, memory, loops, and prompt engineering, noting that directly storing state and calling APIs yourself is preferable to routing through the LLM.

sections.title: Second Demo: Date Night Planning and Closing Remarks
sections.summary: Lasater runs a second demo where the agent plans a Saturday date night with activities and dinner between 6 and 11 p.m. The agent searches for local activities and restaurants, browses the web, marks items done, checks the goal, and outputs suggestions. Lasater acknowledges the agent is not perfect but emphasizes how the components coming together produce interesting behavior. He suggests next steps such as adding a vector database or RAG-like system for browsed web pages. He closes by sharing his LinkedIn, slides on his personal site, and code on GitHub, inviting feedback and collaboration.

demonstrations: Step Zero: standard OpenAI chat completion
Step One: LLM-as-judge condition with forced JSON Boolean response on 'average wing speed of a swallow'
Step Two: Google search tool via SerpAI for buying a hoodie near Time Square, with validation failure on location parameter
Step Three: refactored tool handling with parallel tool call support using Promise.all
Step Four: to-do list planning with browse-web tool (Cheerio and Turndown), system prompt, and agent demo for 'I want to learn about building agents without a framework'

Step Four demo execution: agent searches Google, browses blog posts and Pond Data, converts pages to markdown, marks tasks done, gets LLM-as-judge thumbs up, produces summary of building agents without a framework

Second demo: agent plans a Saturday date night with activities and dinner between 6 and 11 p.m., searches for local activities and restaurants, browses the web, marks items done, checks the goal, outputs suggestions
limitations: Step Two failed due to validation constraint on location parameter requiring specific string values, not arbitrary strings
LLM can iterate forever calling tools and never converge, particularly if context window is pruned and no error or boundary condition is hit
LLM sometimes does not know the current date, requiring it to be added to the prompt
The agent is not perfect by any means, though it produces interesting and useful behavior
